commitments.boundary: Preferring publicly testable methods does not entail that every justified belief must be scientifically testable.
commitments.scope: Public repeatable testing merits greater confidence than a comparably unsupported private method.
commitments.proposition: Public repeatable testing merits greater confidence than a comparably unsupported private method.
nonEntailments: Science is the only source of knowledge
A publicly testable method is infallible or every private experience lacks personal evidential value.
falsePositives: Confidence in science must not be read as denying every nonscientific justification.
Preference between these two methods does not license a general rule that all knowledge must be experimental.

sourceClaims.claim: Intersubjectively ascertainable observations and public theory testing are a recognized rationale for the epistemic credibility of empirical claims; the account also acknowledges theory-ladenness and does not make every private experience worthless.

commitments.label: Defeasible first-person warrant from apparent revelation
commitments.boundary: Only a possible defeasible initial factual reason for the experiencer is inferred. Neither the truth of the message nor substantial standalone justification, independent public or outsider warrant, religious identity, or moral/legal authority follows. EPI021 is excluded because its audience and threshold are ambiguous.
commitments.scope: An apparent divine revelation can sometimes give its experiencer an initial factual reason in favor of its content before independent verification, even if that reason may later be defeated.
commitments.proposition: An apparent divine revelation can sometimes give its experiencer an initial factual reason in favor of its content before independent verification, even if that reason may later be defeated.
nonEntailments: An apparent message is actually divine or true
The respondent has had a revelation
An outsider should believe the content
A revelation can ground public policy
The message has moral or legal authority
falsePositives: EPI021 disagreement need not establish first-person initial warrant because the audience and sufficiency threshold are unspecified.
EPI032 little justification is not a clean denial of all initial factual reasons.
Accepting a reason to investigate is not the same as accepting a factual reason in favor of a message.
Context-dependent warrant does not affirm or deny the unconditional case.

sourceClaims.claim: A recognized account permits an apparent religious experience to give its subject defeasible initial grounds for a factual belief without independent verification; the subject's grounds and an outsider's testimonial grounds are distinct and disputed.
The epistemic status of putative revelation is disputed; revelation as an apparent communication is distinct from the truth of its content and from its authority for outsiders.

commitments.label: Ordinary perceived objects exist independently of minds.
commitments.boundary: Mind-independence is distinct from whether perception is direct or representational and from whether perceptual knowledge is certain.
commitments.scope: Ordinary perceived objects exist independently of minds.
commitments.proposition: Ordinary perceived objects exist independently of minds.
falsePositives: An indirect-perception answer is compatible with an external world.

commitments.label: A non-designer source of objective human purpose is a live plausible possibility.
commitments.boundary: This does not establish that objective purpose actually exists; it concerns a proposed source conditional on that possibility.
commitments.scope: A non-designer source of objective human purpose is a live plausible possibility.
commitments.proposition: A non-designer source of objective human purpose is a live plausible possibility.
nonEntailments: A divine reality does not exist
falsePositives: Choosing a nondivine source as most plausible does not establish objective purpose.

commitments.label: Political decision authority should generally favor smaller or overlapping institutions over uniform central rules.
commitments.boundary: Decentralization is broader than federalism and can be favored for different reasons; this is not a constitutional prescription.
commitments.scope: Political decision authority should generally favor smaller or overlapping institutions over uniform central rules.
commitments.proposition: Political decision authority should generally favor smaller or overlapping institutions over uniform central rules.
falsePositives: The mirror pair is one authored evidence unit, not two independent observations.

commitments.label: In deeply defective institutions, a decisive institutional break can deserve priority over continued gradual reform or continuity.
commitments.boundary: Institutional rupture is not automatically violent revolution, rebellion, resistance, or secession.
commitments.scope: In deeply defective institutions, a decisive institutional break can deserve priority over continued gradual reform or continuity.
commitments.proposition: In deeply defective institutions, a decisive institutional break can deserve priority over continued gradual reform or continuity.
falsePositives: A response to repeatedly failed reforms should not be generalized to every political disagreement.

commitments.label: If divine reality exists, an intentional or personal character is more likely than a wholly impersonal one.
commitments.boundary: This is conditional on divine reality and does not itself establish providence, intervention, or a particular religion.
commitments.scope: If divine reality exists, an intentional or personal character is more likely than a wholly impersonal one.
commitments.proposition: If divine reality exists, an intentional or personal character is more likely than a wholly impersonal one.
falsePositives: Partly mind-like is not a fully personal deity.

commitments.label: A divine or supernatural agent can sometimes influence ordinary events.
commitments.boundary: Belief that intervention is possible is weaker than attributing a particular event to intervention.
commitments.scope: A divine or supernatural agent can sometimes influence ordinary events.
commitments.proposition: A divine or supernatural agent can sometimes influence ordinary events.
nonEntailments: A particular event was an intervention
falsePositives: A natural account of one answered-prayer case does not rule out every intervention.

commitments.label: Events can sometimes occur through miraculous action beyond ordinary natural processes.
commitments.boundary: An unexplained event is not automatically a miracle; agnosticism and preference for unknown natural explanation remain non-directional.
commitments.scope: Events can sometimes occur through miraculous action beyond ordinary natural processes.
commitments.proposition: Events can sometimes occur through miraculous action beyond ordinary natural processes.
falsePositives: An unexplained recovery is not itself proof of a miracle.

commitments.label: Relationships and social roles importantly constitute aspects of personal identity.
commitments.boundary: Relational self-construal can coexist with individual autonomy and is not equivalent to political collectivism.
commitments.scope: Relationships and social roles importantly constitute aspects of personal identity.
commitments.proposition: Relationships and social roles importantly constitute aspects of personal identity.
nonEntailments: A person ceases to exist after losing roles
falsePositives: Some change in social role need not mean a changed core identity.

commitments.label: Group hierarchy can be acceptable even without individual differences that justify it.
commitments.boundary: These custom items are not the SDO-7 and do not justify applying its published norms or cutoffs.
commitments.scope: Group hierarchy can be acceptable even without individual differences that justify it.
commitments.proposition: Group hierarchy can be acceptable even without individual differences that justify it.
falsePositives: Rejecting status merely from supposed superiority is compatible with other hierarchies.

commitments.label: Reducing group-status inequality is not intrinsically important.
commitments.boundary: Anti-egalitarianism is distinct from an explicit desire for one group to dominate another.
commitments.scope: Reducing group-status inequality is not intrinsically important.
commitments.proposition: Reducing group-status inequality is not intrinsically important.
falsePositives: A concern about unjustified hierarchy does not settle whether equality matters in itself.

commitments.label: People generally tend to receive fortunes that correspond to what they deserve.
commitments.boundary: General just-world belief is distinct from personal just-world belief and does not by itself establish victim blaming.
commitments.scope: People generally tend to receive fortunes that correspond to what they deserve.
commitments.proposition: People generally tend to receive fortunes that correspond to what they deserve.
falsePositives: Believing justice desirable is not believing it generally happens.

commitments.label: Character contributes to moral assessment
commitments.boundary: Not sufficient to identify a particular virtue-ethical tradition.
commitments.scope: Character contributes to moral assessment

commitments.label: Psychological egoism
commitments.scope: Descriptive universal claim that ultimate motives concern one’s own welfare. Distinguish desire ownership from desire content.
commitments.boundary: acting on my desires means desiring only my own welfare

commitments.label: Determinism excludes free choice
commitments.scope: If a choice is fixed by the complete prior state of the world and the laws of nature, it cannot be genuinely free.
commitments.boundary: A conditional about determined choices and freedom, not a belief that determinism is true, that free will exists, or that moral responsibility requires free will. AHI104 tests necessary alternatives and is excluded from this broad rule. Disagreement with the reasons-and-capacities sufficient condition in AHI105 is nondirectional.
commitments.proposition: If a choice is fixed by the complete prior state of the world and the laws of nature, it cannot be genuinely free.

sourceClaims.claim: The free-will incompatibilist denies that a choice fixed by the complete prior state and laws can be free; this conditional does not assert that determinism is actually true or settle moral responsibility.
Compatibilist theories can allow free choice under determinism, while the alternatives-possibilities and sourcehood debates do not collapse into a single necessary condition.

nonEntailments: The respondent has or lacks free will
falsePositives: Rejecting one reasons-and-capacities sufficient condition does not establish that every determined choice is unfree.
Requiring alternative possibilities is a narrower route to incompatibilism; two near-paraphrases cannot count as independent authored support.
A belief about whether determinism is true does not answer the conditional compatibility question.

commitments.label: Fallibilism about knowledge
commitments.scope: Whether knowledge can coexist with the possibility of error; distinct from willingness to revise, skepticism, and infallibility of a nonpropositional perceptual process.
commitments.boundary: fallible judgments disqualify Objectivism; fallibilism denies knowledge
commitments.proposition: A claim can count as knowledge even when its justification leaves open a possibility of error.

sourceClaims.claim: Fallibilistic knowledge can be knowledge even when its justification does not conclusively eliminate possible error; this need not imply skepticism.

commitments.label: Pragmatic method for conceptual disputes
commitments.scope: Disputed ideas should be clarified through their conceivable effects on experience or conduct; if two formulations have no conceivable difference in those effects, their apparent conceptual difference is not substantive.
commitments.boundary: The rule requires both endorsement of clarifying a disputed idea by conceivable experience or conduct and rejection of a substantive conceptual difference where no such difference is conceivable. Treating consequences as merely helpful, fallibilism, empirical testing, and disagreement with an absolute reverse item do not establish the conjunction.
commitments.proposition: Disputed ideas should be clarified through their conceivable effects on experience or conduct; if two formulations have no conceivable difference in those effects, their apparent conceptual difference is not substantive.

sourceClaims.claim: Peirce and James used a pragmatic method to clarify concepts by their conceivable experiential or practical bearings and to expose apparently empty disputes; their views of truth and realism still differ.

neighbors: Consequences as one useful clarification technique
Metaphysical realism with no conceivable practical difference
nonEntailments: A belief is true because it is useful
All meaningful language is exhaustively reducible to observation
falsePositives: EPI104 agreement only questions the substance of a dispute; it does not settle the stronger method.
EPI105 disagreement rejects an absolute reverse claim and can come from non-pragmatists.
EPI123 reason_to_question_only treats consequences as a clue rather than settling the conceptual dispute.
EPI103 agreement alone can express a useful technique without accepting the empty-dispute consequence.
Fallibilism and scientific testing do not entail the pragmatic maxim.

commitments.label: Concepts as revisable instruments of inquiry
commitments.scope: Conceptual revision and usefulness in inquiry; compatible with constraints from mind-independent reality.
commitments.boundary: human-made concepts entail arbitrary truth; revising definitions excludes Rand

commitments.label: Noninferential foundations of justification
commitments.scope: Whether some epistemic warrant is not derived from other beliefs. Foundationalism need not make every foundation infallible.
commitments.boundary: foundationalism entails infallibility; anti-foundationalism equals pragmatism

commitments.label: Contextual certainty
commitments.scope: Whether sufficient evidence in a context can warrant certainty despite possible later revision. Not dogmatic immunity to evidence.
commitments.boundary: certainty necessarily means timeless immunity to correction

commitments.label: Perceptual-conceptual basis of factual warrant
commitments.scope: Grounding claims about the concrete external world in sensory evidence integrated by reasoning; not a priori rationalism or rejecting scientific inference.
commitments.boundary: reason alone means a priori deduction; indirect inference lacks sensory grounding
commitments.proposition: Knowledge claims about concrete external reality ultimately require experiential evidence; reasoning alone cannot establish new external-world facts.

sourceClaims.claim: A subject-scoped empiricist thesis about the external world makes experiential evidence the ultimate source of knowledge of external facts, without excluding reasoning about that evidence.

commitments.label: Human-life grounding of moral standards
commitments.scope: Whether requirements of human life and flourishing ground objective moral standards. Separate from mere biological description or current preferences.
commitments.boundary: moral realism entails a human-nature ethic; atheism entails objective egoism

commitments.label: Choice-to-live conditionality of moral reasons
commitments.scope: Whether moral requirements are conditional on choosing to live. This is not identical to making morality relative to any passing desire.
commitments.boundary: denying categorical reasons rules out Rand; hypothetical reasons imply cultural relativism

commitments.label: Exclusive moral self-priority
commitments.scope: Each person morally ought to make their own long-term good the ultimate end of their actions; another person’s need alone supplies no independent moral reason.
commitments.boundary: The rule requires both a universal own-good moral end and denial that another person’s need alone supplies an independent moral reason. Endorsing self-care or a personal prerogative, denying a duty while accepting an independent reason, and psychologically self-interested motivation do not satisfy it.
commitments.proposition: Each person morally ought to make their own long-term good the ultimate end of their actions; another person’s need alone supplies no independent moral reason.

sourceClaims.claim: Ethical egoism is a normative claim about each agent’s own good as the ultimate end. It differs from psychological egoism, rational egoism, ordinary self-regard, and permission for personal projects; helping others can be chosen for self-interested reasons.

neighbors: Ethical egoism as a maximizing rightness theory
nonEntailments: People in fact always pursue their own good
Each action is right if and only if it best advances the agent’s own good
The respondent would refuse to help anyone
The respondent is indifferent to others
Egoists cannot cooperate or aid others for self-interested reasons
A particular view of politics, markets, or rights
falsePositives: NEI100 and NEI101 paraphrase the own-good priority and cannot independently establish denial of another person’s moral reason.
NEI102 disagreement can reflect rejection of its wording without affirming exclusive moral self-priority.
NEI121 independent_reason denies a duty but affirms a moral reason and therefore opposes the exclusive proposition.
NEI121 own_good_only alone does not establish the universal own-good moral end or Rand’s specific life-grounded ethics.
NEI121 context_matters is not directional evidence.

commitments.label: Rational egoism about practical reasons
commitments.scope: Whether one’s own welfare supplies the ultimate standard of practical rationality; distinct from moral rightness and descriptive motivation.
commitments.boundary: rational egoism equals psychological egoism

commitments.label: Ownness and revisable allegiance to ideals
commitments.scope: Original operationalization of non-subjection to fixed ideals and revisable appropriation of projects. An interpretive proposal, not a validated Stirner scale.
commitments.boundary: ownness entails compulsive selfishness; ownness entails inability to love; ownness dictates a specific economic institution

commitments.label: Promissory self-binding
commitments.scope: Whether a voluntary promise itself creates a defeasible reason beyond current desire; not an exceptionless duty or legal remedy rule.
commitments.boundary: promissory reasons are always overriding; legal enforceability proves moral duty

commitments.label: Continuing endorsement and exit from commitments
commitments.scope: Whether continued association or service requires renewed endorsement; separate from duties to repair induced reliance and from valid waiver.
commitments.boundary: exit entails no compensation; withdrawal entails endorsement of fraud

commitments.label: Reliance-based reasons for performance or repair
commitments.scope: Reasons generated by induced expectations and reliance; separable from promises as normative powers and from specific-performance enforcement.
commitments.boundary: rejecting promise-based duties rejects reliance duties; repair requires compelled personal service

commitments.label: Elective other-regarding concern
commitments.scope: Possibility of voluntarily caring about another as an end without making universal self-sacrifice a duty. Not the intensity of experienced affection.
commitments.boundary: rejection of obligatory altruism entails no affection; voluntary caring proves hidden self-interest

commitments.label: Abstract-object commitment
commitments.scope: Existence of abstract objects such as numbers, distinct from realism about universals and ordinary physical objects.
commitments.boundary: abstract objects equal universals; abstract-object denial entails denial of tables

commitments.label: Universals commitment
commitments.scope: Whether numerically the same universal is instantiated by distinct things; separate from shared resemblance and mental concepts.
commitments.boundary: rejecting universals denies objective resemblance; concept theory settles all abstract ontology

commitments.label: Ordinary external-world independence
commitments.scope: Independence of ordinary concrete objects from thought; does not settle social ontology, universals, or the method of ontology.
commitments.boundary: world realism entails abstract realism; social construction entails idealism

commitments.label: Easy or deflationary approach to ontology
commitments.scope: Using conceptual application conditions and ordinary empirical inquiry rather than an additional heavyweight existence test. Compatibility with realism remains disputed.
commitments.boundary: easy ontology entails nominalism; deflationary method denies existence
commitments.proposition: Some existence questions can be settled by a concept’s ordinary application conditions together with relevant empirical facts, without an additional distinctively metaphysical existence test.

sourceClaims.claim: Marschall describes Easy Ontology as settling many ontological questions through conceptual truths and empirical knowledge, while disputing whether its defense of realism succeeds.

commitments.label: Preinstitutional grounding of rights
commitments.scope: Whether persons have basic rights independently of social recognition; distinct from the form and strength of a particular property regime.
commitments.boundary: strong rights entail one unique moral foundation; natural rights entail a state

commitments.label: Institutional and instrumental justification of rights
commitments.scope: Justification of rights in terms of agency, cooperation or institutional consequences. May coexist with status-based justification.
commitments.boundary: instrumental justification entails weak rights; instrumental rights entail utilitarianism

commitments.label: Territorial monopoly of final legal force
commitments.scope: Whether a single final rights-protecting legal authority is necessary within a territory. Separate from arbitrary command and unqualified obedience.
commitments.boundary: rights protection entails general duty to obey all laws; philosophical anarchism entails rejecting courts

commitments.label: Nonstate adjudication and protective provision
commitments.scope: Institutional possibility and acceptability of nonstate legal services; separate from rejection of general political obligation and from assuming all commons require markets.
commitments.boundary: polycentricity entails total state abolition; nonstate provision proves all practical cases succeed

commitments.label: Institutional value independent of obedience
commitments.scope: Practical justification and participation without conceding a general content-independent moral duty. Not a disguised abolition scale.
commitments.boundary: no general obedience implies no useful public institutions

commitments.label: Institutional state-abolition preference
commitments.scope: Preference for replacing states, independent of rejecting general obligation. This does not measure timing or methods of transition.
commitments.boundary: philosophical anarchism entails immediate abolition; abolition entails violent methods

commitments.label: Contractual remedies distinct from continuing assent
commitments.scope: Justification of compensatory or protective remedies despite withdrawal, distinct from compulsory personal performance or legal advice about existing law.
commitments.boundary: withdrawal permission rules out remedies; enforceability proves moral promise theories

commitments.label: Institutional dependence without elimination
commitments.scope: Whether institution-dependent entities can be real; different from independence from all persons or a moral collective duty.
commitments.boundary: social dependence entails fiction; social entities entail moral collectivism

commitments.label: Individual-level explanation of social processes
commitments.scope: Whether social explanations must be grounded in agents and their interactions; not normative individualism or denial of aggregate patterns.
commitments.boundary: methodological individualism entails selfishness; group agency entails collectivist morality

commitments.label: Projects and relationships can create meaning
commitments.boundary: Can coexist with objective meaning; absence of cosmic purpose is not pessimism.
commitments.scope: Projects and relationships can create meaning

commitments.label: The same total state and laws fix one future
commitments.boundary: Does not establish incompatibilism or remove moral responsibility.
commitments.scope: The same total state and laws fix one future

commitments.label: Some divine reality probably exists
commitments.boundary: Neither religious practice nor support for religious law is inferred.
commitments.scope: Some divine reality probably exists

commitments.label: Effective opportunities matter to freedom
commitments.boundary: Does not establish socialism, authoritarianism or a particular distribution policy.
commitments.scope: Effective opportunities matter to freedom

commitments.label: Cognitive systems can include external tools
commitments.boundary: A useful tool is not automatically part of a mind. This is a narrow reported judgment.
commitments.scope: Cognitive systems can include external tools

commitments.label: Equal interests count without personal proximity
commitments.boundary: Neither willingness to harm nor a utilitarian identity follows.
commitments.scope: Equal interests count without personal proximity

commitments.label: Instrumental harm can be permissible
commitments.boundary: These scenarios do not measure all consequentialist commitments; exceptional answers remain qualified.
commitments.scope: Instrumental harm can be permissible

commitments.label: market-coordination
commitments.scope: Your preferences between voluntary exchange, prices and deliberate allocation in the stated coordination cases.
commitments.boundary: Coordination preferences do not establish Objectivism, an ethical code or a universal case for one institution. Markets, states and commons can be evaluated differently by activity.

commitments.label: moral-truth-aptness
commitments.scope: Your explicit answers about whether moral sentences can be true or false.
commitments.boundary: Truth-aptness does not establish stance-independent moral truth or an Objectivist identity. Expressivist and quasi-realist accounts can accommodate truth-talk; expressing an attitude need not deny every kind of truth-aptness.

commitments.label: no-general-obedience
commitments.scope: The philosophical-anarchist position about a general content-independent duty to obey, not a policy of immediate institutional abolition.
commitments.boundary: Inherited narrow criterion; do not generalize it beyond The philosophical-anarchist position about a general content-independent duty to obey, not a policy of immediate institutional abolition.

commitments.label: Moral relevance of authority
commitments.scope: Reported importance of authority in moral assessment, without assigning a party or philosophical system.
commitments.boundary: Not an administration or validation of MFQ-2; other concerns can be high simultaneously.

commitments.label: Moral relevance of care
commitments.scope: Reported importance of care in moral assessment, without assigning a party or philosophical system.
commitments.boundary: Not an administration or validation of MFQ-2; other concerns can be high simultaneously.

commitments.label: Moral relevance of equality
commitments.scope: Reported importance of equality in moral assessment, without assigning a party or philosophical system.
commitments.boundary: Not an administration or validation of MFQ-2; other concerns can be high simultaneously.

commitments.label: Moral relevance of loyalty
commitments.scope: Reported importance of loyalty in moral assessment, without assigning a party or philosophical system.
commitments.boundary: Not an administration or validation of MFQ-2; other concerns can be high simultaneously.

commitments.label: Moral relevance of proportionality
commitments.scope: Reported importance of proportionality in moral assessment, without assigning a party or philosophical system.
commitments.boundary: Not an administration or validation of MFQ-2; other concerns can be high simultaneously.

commitments.label: Moral relevance of purity
commitments.scope: Reported importance of purity in moral assessment, without assigning a party or philosophical system.
commitments.boundary: Not an administration or validation of MFQ-2; other concerns can be high simultaneously.

commitments.label: Moral constraints can limit beneficial actions
commitments.boundary: Threshold exceptions and absolute prohibitions remain different.
commitments.scope: Moral constraints can limit beneficial actions

commitments.label: Extreme injustice may undermine legal status
commitments.boundary: A limited natural-law comparison, not a complete religious or political identity.
commitments.scope: Extreme injustice may undermine legal status

commitments.label: Mutual advantage helps justify moral rules
commitments.boundary: Other justifications may coexist; choosing another reason is not counted as rejection.
commitments.scope: Mutual advantage helps justify moral rules

commitments.label: Reality is entirely natural
commitments.boundary: Atheism, science preference and reductionism are not substitutes for these answers.
commitments.scope: Reality is entirely natural

commitments.label: Uncontrolled power itself can diminish freedom
commitments.boundary: Do not infer arbitrary control from every dependence or infer a complete republican ideology.
commitments.scope: Uncontrolled power itself can diminish freedom

commitments.label: Interference with harmless choice reduces liberty
commitments.boundary: Does not select a party, economic system, or position on all positive freedoms.
commitments.scope: Interference with harmless choice reduces liberty

commitments.label: Meaning can exceed subjective experience
commitments.boundary: Not necessarily divine purpose, religion or an objective-list theory of welfare.
commitments.scope: Meaning can exceed subjective experience

commitments.label: Consequences count as moral reasons
commitments.boundary: Does not establish exclusive consequentialism or aggregate maximization.
commitments.scope: Consequences count as moral reasons

commitments.label: Aesthetic value can exceed actual liking
commitments.boundary: This narrow aesthetic-objectivity comparison is not a claim about moral truth or a correct artistic taste.
commitments.scope: Aesthetic value can exceed actual liking. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Simple physical systems may have basic experience
commitments.boundary: This is a limited panpsychism-related comparison, not a claim that every object thinks like a person.
commitments.scope: Simple physical systems may have basic experience. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Strong contrary evidence should reopen beliefs
commitments.boundary: A revisable belief need not be weakly supported. Contextual certainty and fallibility are not treated as simple opposites.
commitments.scope: Strong contrary evidence should reopen beliefs. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Moral reasons need not serve existing desires
commitments.boundary: A reason to act, actual motivation and an overriding obligation are separate. An answer about one does not supply the others.
commitments.scope: Moral reasons need not serve existing desires. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: A coherent web helps ground justification
commitments.boundary: This comparison is about justification, not truth being whatever a group agrees on.
commitments.scope: A coherent web helps ground justification. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Other possible worlds are concrete realities
commitments.boundary: Rejecting concrete worlds does not identify one alternative. Merely considering possibilities does not endorse concrete-world realism.
commitments.scope: Other possible worlds are concrete realities. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Conscious reasoning can genuinely affect action
commitments.boundary: Caused reasoning can still be reasoning. This does not require uncaused choices or reject unconscious influences.
commitments.scope: Conscious reasoning can genuinely affect action. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Consent is central to legitimate political coercion
commitments.boundary: Explicit, tacit and hypothetical consent differ. This does not infer state abolition or a duty to obey all laws.
commitments.scope: Consent is central to legitimate political coercion. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Context can change the appropriate moral judgment
commitments.boundary: Exceptions and context sensitivity do not entail relativism or the absence of moral principles.
commitments.scope: Context can change the appropriate moral judgment. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Human life participates in purpose built into reality
commitments.boundary: Does not establish objective moral requirements, a personal deity or felt meaning in someone’s life.
commitments.scope: Human life participates in purpose built into reality. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Participation adds to political legitimacy
commitments.boundary: Democratic authorization is not a view about workplace ownership or a license to override all rights.
commitments.scope: Participation adds to political legitimacy. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Desert can justify punishment without future benefit
commitments.boundary: Desert is distinct from deterrence and the permissibility of excessive punishment.
commitments.scope: Desert can justify punishment without future benefit. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Informed desire fulfillment can improve well-being
commitments.boundary: Choosing another account is not blanket opposition to desire fulfillment. This does not identify ethical egoism.
commitments.scope: Informed desire fulfillment can improve well-being. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Causing harm can be worse than failing to prevent it
commitments.boundary: An equally-wrong verdict can arise from further duties; it is not automatically counted as rejecting every doing/allowing distinction.
commitments.scope: Causing harm can be worse than failing to prevent it. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Past and future events are as real as present events
commitments.boundary: Opposition does not establish presentism: growing block and other accounts remain. Eternalism does not itself establish fatalism or determinism.
commitments.scope: Past and future events are as real as present events. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Relevant expert agreement can be evidence
commitments.boundary: Trust in relevant expertise does not imply technocratic rule, infallible experts or uncritical deference.
commitments.scope: Relevant expert agreement can be evidence. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Mental content can partly depend on the environment
commitments.boundary: Content externalism differs from an extended cognitive system and does not imply group priority.
commitments.scope: Mental content can partly depend on the environment. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Some justification rests on basic beliefs or experiences
commitments.boundary: Choosing another account does not reject every foundational element. Basic beliefs need not be infallible.
commitments.scope: Some justification rests on basic beliefs or experiences. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Higher-level properties are fully reducible in principle
commitments.boundary: Irreducibility need not mean supernaturalism. The question concerns a general explanatory commitment, not established scientific reduction.
commitments.scope: Higher-level properties are fully reducible in principle. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Functional organization can determine mental states
commitments.boundary: Functional roles and implementation are distinct questions. Other theory choices do not automatically refute all functional claims.
commitments.scope: Functional organization can determine mental states. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Natural laws do more than summarize events
commitments.boundary: Dispositionalism remains an alternative, not a midpoint or rejection of every non-Humean account.
commitments.scope: Natural laws do more than summarize events. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Groups can meaningfully have goals
commitments.boundary: Group agency is not the normative thesis that groups may override individual rights.
commitments.scope: Groups can meaningfully have goals. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Very large benefits can require major sacrifice
commitments.boundary: This reports demanding obligations, not how much a respondent actually donates or whether they accept utilitarianism.
commitments.scope: Very large benefits can require major sacrifice. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Laws depend on the total pattern of particular events
commitments.boundary: This narrow Humean-law comparison does not imply moral Humeanism, empiricism or deterministic physics.
commitments.scope: Laws depend on the total pattern of particular events. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Individuals have claims against group override
commitments.boundary: Not a denial of social dependence, group agency or the existence of institutions.
commitments.scope: Individuals have claims against group override. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Some purposes are built into nature
commitments.boundary: Purpose in nature is distinct from a personal creator, ethical purpose and a felt meaningful life.
commitments.scope: Some purposes are built into nature. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

commitments.label: Intention matters beyond foreseeable consequences
commitments.boundary: This does not establish the full doctrine of double effect. Intention and doing/allowing are not interchangeable.
commitments.scope: Intention matters beyond foreseeable consequences. Interpreted only in the contexts of these questions.

sourceClaims.claim: Cognitivist accounts treat ordinary moral sentences as truth-apt and their acceptance as belief-like. commitments.scope: Some ordinary moral wrongness statements make claims that can literally be true or false.

A complete account of moral judgment as belief

commitments.label: An act’s own consequences ultimately determine its moral rightness, and an available act with a better outcome for everyone affected rules out a worse act as permissible.

sourceClaims.claim: Act consequentialism applies the moral-rightness criterion directly to an act’s own consequences; in its maximizing form, an act is right only when its outcome is at least as good as the outcomes of available alternatives. This differs from full rule consequentialism, which makes wrongness depend on consequence-justified rules (sections 1, 2, and 5).

commitments.boundary: The generic claim that outcomes matter is not decisive evidence. The rule-outcome option and the possibility of permitting a worse act prevent a direct maximizing-act inference. This does not identify utilitarianism or settle what counts as good.
commitments.scope: An act’s own consequences ultimately determine its moral rightness, and an available act with a better outcome for everyone affected rules out a worse act as permissible.
commitments.proposition: An act’s own consequences ultimately determine its moral rightness, and an available act with a better outcome for everyone affected rules out a worse act as permissible.
falsePositives: Taking consequences seriously does not say they exclusively determine rightness.
Rejecting a rule in one case without rejecting permissible worse-outcome acts does not satisfy both evidence units.
A rule chosen for its good consequences is still a rule criterion, not automatically a direct act criterion.

commitments.label: An act’s moral rightness depends on conformity to rules ultimately justified by their consequences, even when that act alone would produce a better outcome.

sourceClaims.claim: For a full rule-consequentialist criterion of wrongness, acts are wrong when forbidden by rules justified by their consequences. This differs from using consequence-justified rules merely as a decision procedure while direct act outcomes determine wrongness (sections 4 and 8).

commitments.boundary: Consequences that make a rule useful do not alone make that rule the criterion of an act’s rightness. Selecting reasonable agreement is not treated as opposition because contractualist and consequence-based justifications can overlap. This does not measure rules for blame or a full rule-consequentialist identity.
commitments.scope: An act’s moral rightness depends on conformity to rules ultimately justified by their consequences, even when that act alone would produce a better outcome.
commitments.proposition: An act’s moral rightness depends on conformity to rules ultimately justified by their consequences, even when that act alone would produce a better outcome.
falsePositives: A useful rule of thumb can be endorsed by someone who judges rightness directly from each act’s outcome.

commitments.label: Welfare as the only ultimate outcome good

sourceClaims.claim: Welfarism makes well-being the only ultimate value; accepting this value thesis does not by itself settle rights, equality, or a criterion of right action.
A welfarist theory of outcome value differs from plural theories that recognize beauty, truth, justice, or other goods independently of individual welfare.
The possible independent value of nonhuman nature provides a genuine counterexample to welfare-only outcome value, but this one question does not identify an environmental theory.

commitments.boundary: This is about ultimate outcome value. It neither says that the right act maximizes welfare nor that rights, promises, fairness, or other duties cannot constrain action. One denial of unseen beauty alone does not establish the general thesis.
commitments.scope: Only how well affected beings fare ultimately makes an outcome better or worse in itself; beauty does not add independent outcome value when no being’s well-being changes.
commitments.proposition: Only how well affected beings fare ultimately makes an outcome better or worse in itself; beauty does not add independent outcome value when no being’s well-being changes.

nonEntailments: A duty to maximize aggregate welfare

Equal weighting, a simple total, or any population aggregation rule
The absence of independent value in every untested case

Act-utilitarian accounts can explain promissory obligations through the welfare effects of promises and their breach, while rule-utilitarian accounts evaluate general promise-keeping practices; a promise conflict is a discriminator rather than a complete theory label.

The criterion of rightness is distinct from the theory of outcome value and from total-versus-average aggregation; this release measures only the explicit total-well-being commitment tested in its authored items.

constructs.name: Free-will belief
constructs.auditRationale: Current free-will items partly encode compatibilist conditions, so disagreement may mean incompatibilism rather than disbelief in free will.
constructs.coverageGap: Compatibilist conditions cannot be used as denials of free will by incompatibilists.

constructs.name: Moral-responsibility belief
constructs.auditRationale: Current items directly address basic/desert-entailing responsibility and manipulation; keep distinct from forward-looking responsibility.
constructs.coverageGap: A manipulated action and causal explanation do not negate the possibility of desert in other actions.

constructs.name: Baseline human benevolence
constructs.auditRationale: The broad 'baseline benevolence' label overreaches. Existing direct items can support only the narrower claim that humans are capable of genuinely other-regarding motivation.
constructs.coverageGap: Capacity for altruism and frequency of benevolent action differ; disagreeing with often does not deny capacity.

constructs.name: Baseline human selfishness / competition
constructs.auditRationale: Self-interest prevalence and competition are different. Psychological egoism is already represented by AH13 and social competition by SO08; do not score this bundled construct as one worldview dimension.
constructs.coverageGap: Self-interest, psychological egoism, and competition are distinct claims; the current items bundle them.

constructs.name: Human-nature mutability
constructs.auditRationale: Existing items directly concern malleability of human dispositions; keep separate from whether causes are biological or environmental.
constructs.coverageGap: Change in some dispositions can coexist with stability in others; the apparent opposites have different quantifiers.

constructs.name: Human-nature complexity
constructs.auditRationale: A generic preference for multi-causal explanation is a methodological outlook with no clear validated worldview construct here; retain for research only.
constructs.coverageGap: Multicausal explanation is an exploratory methodological variable, not an interpreted human-nature factor.

constructs.name: Biological causal attribution
constructs.auditRationale: Interpret only the reported belief that biological/inherited factors can make substantial causal contributions; do not infer immutability or normativity.

constructs.name: Environmental / social causal attribution
constructs.auditRationale: Interpret only the reported belief that social/environmental factors can substantially shape behavior; do not infer blank-slate views.

constructs.name: Agency theory family
constructs.auditRationale: Compatibilist/libertarian/skeptical family classification must remain derived from free-will, determinism, and responsibility answers.
constructs.coverageGap: Freedom-theory families require joint free-will, determinism, and responsibility evidence.

constructs.name: Incompatibilist condition on free agency
constructs.auditRationale: AHI104 is a near-parallel necessary-alternatives claim. AHI108 asks the compatibility question under favorable deliberation conditions; AHI105 agreement can oppose, but disagreement is nondirectional.

constructs.name: Knowledge complexity
constructs.auditRationale: Existing items directly ask whether knowledge is simple versus interconnected/developing; interpret only this narrow personal-epistemology proposition.

constructs.name: Attainability of truth
constructs.auditRationale: EPI015 was already excluded and the remaining material does not provide two independent negative indicators of truth attainability without conflating approximation, skepticism, and conventionalism.
constructs.coverageGap: The existing answer set confounds knowledge with certainty and domain-limited skepticism.

constructs.name: Rational / a priori reliance
constructs.auditRationale: Two direct, opposing items support a narrow a-priori-justification interpretation; EPI025 remains excluded as a knowledge/trivia recognition question.
constructs.coverageGap: New observation, all empirical support, and substantive knowledge differ; the existing pair is not converse evidence.

constructs.name: Scientific-method reliance
constructs.auditRationale: Public systematic testability can be interpreted as an epistemic preference, without claiming science is the only source of knowledge.

constructs.name: Revelation as epistemic source
constructs.auditRationale: EPI021 has ambiguous audience and threshold. EPI032 and EPI122 ask for first-person factual reasons; some and substantial EPI032 responses support a modest initial warrant, while little and contextual answers stay nondirectional.
constructs.coverageGap: Outsider/public warrant, substantial standalone justification, and inferential or testimonial revelation remain separate unmeasured or partially measured distinctions.

constructs.name: External-world stance
constructs.auditRationale: The current construct conflates external-world metaphysics, perceptual directness, and skepticism. Retain narrower external-world-independence and skepticism interpretations; do not emit one categorical label.

constructs.name: Pragmatic clarification through consequences
constructs.auditRationale: EPI103 asks for the positive clarification method; EPI123 distinguishes an empty conceptual dispute from merely finding consequences useful. EPI104 is too tentative and EPI105 has an absolute reverse false positive.
constructs.coverageGap: The rule assesses a scoped method, not a theory of truth, the entire pragmatist tradition, or exclusive philosophical identity.

constructs.name: Concepts as revisable instruments of inquiry
Objective-purpose source
constructs.auditRationale: Designer-grounded and non-designer sources of objective purpose should be separate commitments, not one categorical score.

constructs.name: Existential nihilism
constructs.auditRationale: Current items directly distinguish denial of objective/inherent meaning from alternative objective or constructed sources.
constructs.coverageGap: A hypothetical without cosmic purpose cannot establish actual-world nihilism; nondivine objective meaning is another live view.

constructs.name: World safety
constructs.auditRationale: World-safety is a validated Primal World Beliefs construct, but these are custom items and should remain explicitly exploratory until calibrated.
constructs.coverageGap: World safety is an exploratory primal belief here; custom items are not a validated scale.

constructs.name: World aliveness / intentional character
constructs.auditRationale: World-aliveness is a validated primal family, but these custom items mix felt intentionality and metaphysical responsiveness; retain as research-only.
constructs.coverageGap: Perceived world responsiveness is exploratory and not evidence of a philosophical identity.

constructs.name: Optimism vs resignation

constructs.coverageGap: World-improvability items remain exploratory and uncalibrated.

constructs.name: Response to meaninglessness
constructs.auditRationale: Responses to meaninglessness should be derived from meaning/nihilism responses rather than scored as an independent latent trait.
constructs.coverageGap: Existential orientation combines separately interpreted propositions.

constructs.name: Moral truth-aptness

constructs.coverageGap: Actual moral truth, belief-state semantics, and specific noncognitivist theories remain unmeasured.

constructs.name: Metaethical family
constructs.auditRationale: Metaethical family should remain a derived synthesis over independently measured metaethical commitments; MEI005 is diagnostic, not a standalone family scale.
constructs.coverageGap: A metaethical family combines independently interpreted answers; one diagnostic case cannot identify a family.

constructs.name: Liberty / opposition to domination
constructs.auditRationale: Liberty/opposition-to-domination is theoretically interesting, but it is not part of the standard MFQ-2 six-foundation model and the current items are original exploratory content.
constructs.coverageGap: The original domination items are not an administration of MFQ-2 or a calibrated foundation.

constructs.name: Identity under transformation

constructs.coverageGap: Transformation cases can inform a synthesis, but one teleportation scenario does not define a scale.

constructs.name: Ethical egoism as a normative principle
constructs.auditRationale: NEI100 and NEI101 are one authored own-good indicator; NEI121 separately asks whether another person’s need supplies an independent moral reason. NEI102 is not directional evidence for this conjunction.
constructs.coverageGap: The if-and-only-if maximizing rightness thesis, rational egoism, psychological egoism, Stirnerian ownness, and Rand’s life-grounded ethics remain separate.

constructs.name: Ownness and revisable allegiance to ideals

Reliance-based reasons for performance or repair
Direct act-consequence criterion

constructs.name: Consequence-justified rule criterion
constructs.auditRationale: The existing case contrasts act outcome with a consequence-justified rule as criterion; the new question asks what ultimately justifies a rule against harm.

constructs.auditRationale: A general outcome-value choice and an unseen-beauty counterexample jointly distinguish welfare-only value from one major pluralist neighbor while separating act permissions.
constructs.coverageGap: Aggregation, theories of well-being, full value pluralism, and moral rightness remain separate.

constructs.name: Total-well-being maximizing act criterion
constructs.auditRationale: A plain-language general criterion and a distinct promise-conflict application jointly test whether maximizing total well-being is treated as decisive. They are authored evidence units, not empirically independent indicators.
constructs.coverageGap: No full utilitarian theory, account of welfare, distribution rule, broad promise theory, or behavior is inferred.

constructs.name: Metaontology
constructs.auditRationale: Substantive-versus-deflationary attitudes can be reported, but framework relativity and verbalism should not be collapsed into one categorical metaontology label.
constructs.coverageGap: Substantive, framework-relative, and merely verbal disputes are different; the existing frequency claims do not align.

constructs.name: Easy or deflationary approach to ontology

constructs.name: Centralization vs decentralization

constructs.name: Collective / common ownership legitimacy

constructs.name: Reform vs rupture orientation

constructs.name: Social-category essentialism

constructs.name: Belief in social/world justice

limitations: A result concerns explicitly reported commitments under specified wording, never an inferred personal identity.
Published instrument structure or validation does not validate our rewritten items or authorize copied wording.
Disagreement with one proposition does not identify a different school without its own direct evidence.
A tradeoff, dilemma or ranking does not establish a context-free doctrinal preference.
More citations or more profile variants do not add respondent evidence.
Memories, expected identities, demographic categories, country/figure matches and preferred outcomes cannot supply answers.
Metadata-only sources remain references, not reviewed evidence for detailed wording.
The corpus is selected and largely Anglophone; no universal cultural coverage or measurement invariance is claimed.

No generic Buddhism, Hinduism, Confucianism or Indigenous-worldview label may be derived from theism, authority or no-self answers. Dedicated primary scholarship and discriminating items are still required.
Consequence sensitivity and instrumental harm do not measure outcome-only rightness, aggregation, maximizing versus satisficing, and scope well enough to assert full utilitarianism.
The corpus recognizes constructivist objectivity and competing Kantian/Humean variants; the bank lacks sufficient direct procedural-grounding discriminants for a full comparison.
Socialism, liberalism, conservatism and religious traditions have internal variants; policy resemblance alone is insufficient for full-system identities.
Some legacy reverse-keyed items and forced choices contain insufficient-conditions or ambiguity problems; only explicit reviewed mappings enter comparisons.
All repository academic references are inventoried with access limits. This is not all academic literature, all datasets, or proof of universal cultural coverage.
The public form is content-balanced by authored evidence bundles, not selected with empirical item information.
Facets separate kinds of questions within overlapping philosophical fields; ontology is not claimed to be disjoint from metaphysics.
No expert-frequency prior, speed reward, partisan target or personality stereotype is used to choose questions or infer answers.
Presentism, growing-block theory, dispositional laws, abstract modal worlds and several metaethical variants still need better independent discriminants.
The 49-construct audit deliberately leaves derived, research-only, underdiscriminated, and split constructs unresolved rather than forcing 100% mapped coverage.
Psychological validation of cited scales does not transfer to custom Worldview Sorter items; cited measures are conceptual/measurement references only.
Biological, environmental, religious, and political responses are reported as respondent commitments and are not treated as factual truth keys.
The original 49 constructs are an authored theoretical ontology, not empirically established latent factors.
A presented item with no directional answer differs from a proposition never measured on a route.
Single directional authored units are reported only as a lean; no numerical probability or scale score is implied.
A source supporting a conceptual distinction does not validate these custom questions or answer mappings.

Pilot states are authored evidence summaries, not calibrated probabilities, latent-factor estimates, or reliability claims. A rule lacking two available directional units is not measured in this frozen route.

academicUpgradePolicy.meaning: A repeatable review and release procedure, not an autonomous claim to monitor all research.
requirements: Name the philosophical question, its alternatives and cross-loading risks.
Record source URL, reviewed sections, date, access limits and whether evidence is conceptual or empirical.
Map exact item revisions and exact response meanings; keep qualified alternatives and missingness distinct.
Add positive, negative and counterexample regressions before activating an interpretation.
Version the model and selection policy; material wording changes require a new item revision and bank/instrument release.
Replay historical answers only against compatible bank versions; preserve the original snapshots.
Test public form content coverage in addition to item counts, and verify the browser shows it.
Treat study populations, language, incentives and response format as limits on empirical transfer.
caveats: A minimum of two authored evidence groups is an engineering display rule, not reliability or factor identification.
Domain coverage is partial and largely Anglophone. No inference of Buddhist, Confucian, Hindu, Indigenous or other traditions from superficial similarity.
The PhilPapers design is an organizational reference. Expert prevalence is not a truth key, classification prior or population norm.
